title: When Criticizing, Good Leaders Separate the Person From the Opinion
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that people struggle to separate their opinions from their sense of self, which turns most criticism of ideas into perceived personal attacks. The author's central recommendation is that leaders draw a hard line between the person and the opinion when disagreeing, without denying who originated the idea. It offers side-by-side phrasing examples showing how naming a colleague while criticizing their idea changes the emotional register of the feedback compared to critiquing the idea alone. The piece suggests this is a small, learnable habit — omitting personal references when voicing disagreement — that reduces defensive reactions and keeps the conversation focused on the merits of the idea rather than its source.
points: People struggle to separate their opinions from their personal identity, making criticism feel personal.
Good leaders deliberately draw a line between an idea and the person who proposed it when disagreeing.
Naming a colleague while criticizing their idea intensifies the perceived attack, even unintentionally.
Phrasing criticism around the idea alone, without attribution, reduces defensive reactions.
This is described as a small habit change with an outsized effect on how disagreement lands.
quotes: People have an exceedingly difficult time separating their opinions from their personal identities.
Good leaders presume it is their job to draw a hard line between opinions and people to alleviate the need for people to defend themselves.

There is a marked difference between saying, “I don’t think that idea is reasonable or cost-effective,” versus saying, “Kris, I’m not sure why you would propose something that is unreasonable and cost-prohibitive.
Whenever a leader conflates an idea or opinion they don’t like with the person offering it, they set the stage for a defensive reaction — or worse.
Instead, they focus their attention exclusively on the opinion or idea without mention of the source.
When it comes to criticizing an idea or opinion, the best leaders know a sound diagnosis focuses on the issue, not the person.
